Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

ISLAMABAD, Pakistan (CNN)  -- A suspected missile strike from a U.S. Predator drone killed at least four people in a house in Pakistan's North Waziristan region early Saturday. Marchers protest recent U.S. missile strikes on the Pakistani tribal areas. The attack, which occurred in the Mir Ali subdivision in the village of Ali Khel, was one of several to hit the country Saturday. Six people were injured in Saturday's attack, the fourth suspected U.S. strike on Pakistani soil in November. The names of the victims have not been released. It is also not known why the house was targeted. Elsewhere, three people were killed and 11 were injured in an explosion inside a mosque in northwest Pakistan's tribal region, a government official said. The explosion happened just after 4 p.m. (6 a.m. ET), leaving the Hangu district mosque inside Pakistan's North-West Frontier Province in ruins, said Omer Faraz Khan, deputy superintendent of Hangu. He said rescuers were trying to save people trapped under the debris. It was not immediately clear how many people were inside the mosque at the time of the blast. Police were investigating the explosion, which was detonated using a homemade timer, Khan said. Hours later, three bombs exploded about 10 p.m. (noon ET) outside a stadium in Lahore where a music festival was being held, police Inspector Muntzir Kazmi said. A 13-year-old was injured, but it was unknown whether the victim was a boy or girl. This week, Pakistan's Foreign Ministry summoned U.S. Ambassador Anne Patterson to lodge a formal protest against another suspected U.S. missile strike on its territory, an act Pakistan Prime Minister Yousaf Raza Gilani called a violation of his nation's sovereignty.  Watch Gilani say his country has had enough of U.S. attacks » . Wednesday's strike in the Bannu region of Pakistan's North-West Frontier Province left five dead and seven wounded. That attack was farther inside Pakistani territory than previous attacks. The attack targeted a home outside the tribal areas that U.S. intelligence says have become a haven for Taliban and al Qaeda fighters battling U.S. and NATO troops in neighboring Afghanistan. The U.S. government has not acknowledged hitting targets within Pakistan, an ally in the war on al Qaeda launched after the September 11 attacks on New York and Washington. However, Pakistan's government has repeatedly complained about the strikes. Gilani took to the floor of the parliament and renewed his condemnation of the attacks Thursday but added that he thinks they will be controlled when President-elect Barack Obama takes office. In October, the foreign ministry summoned Patterson to lodge a "strong" protest on continuing missile attacks and said they should be stopped immediately. At the time, a missile strike from a suspected U.S. drone on a compound in South Waziristan killed 20 people. Pakistan's government said the attacks cost lives and undermine public support for its counterterrorism efforts. The U.S.-led coalition and NATO, based in Afghanistan, have been seeking a way to effectively battle militants who are launching attacks from Pakistan's swath of tribal areas along the border. They have become frustrated with Islamabad over the years, saying it is not being active enough against militants, a claim Pakistan denies. The United States is the only country operating in the region known to have the capability to launch missiles from drones, which are controlled remotely.

# Escalating Violence Rocks Pakistan Amid Drone Strikes and Bombings

Pakistan experienced a wave of deadly violence, with a suspected U.S. Predator drone strike, a mosque bombing, and an attack outside a music festival all occurring within a short span of time, further straining the already tense relationship between Washington and Islamabad.

## Drone Strike in North Waziristan

In the early hours of Saturday, a suspected U.S. Predator drone strike targeted a house in the Mir Ali subdivision of North Waziristan, a region long known as a stronghold for militant activity along the Afghan border. The attack killed at least four people and left six others injured. This strike marked the fourth such drone attack carried out in Pakistan during the month of November alone, underscoring the intensifying pace of U.S. military operations in the tribal areas.

## Mosque Bombing in Hangu District

In a separate and unrelated incident, an explosion tore through a mosque in Pakistan's Hangu district. The blast was reportedly triggered by a homemade timer device, resulting in the deaths of three people and injuries to 11 others. In the aftermath, rescue workers scrambled to free individuals trapped beneath the rubble and debris left by the explosion, adding to the chaos and casualties from the day's violence.

## Attack Outside Lahore Music Festival

Later that same night, further violence erupted in the city of Lahore, where three bombs detonated outside a stadium hosting a music festival. The blasts injured a 13-year-old attendee, though the child's gender was not immediately confirmed by authorities. The attack cast a shadow over what was intended to be an evening of entertainment and cultural celebration, highlighting the pervasive threat of violence even in urban centers far from the tribal regions.

## Diplomatic Fallout

The string of drone strikes prompted a strong diplomatic response from Islamabad. Pakistan's Foreign Ministry lodged a formal protest with U.S. Ambassador Anne Patterson, objecting to a previous missile strike conducted on Pakistani soil. Prime Minister Yousaf Raza Gilani publicly condemned the attacks, characterizing them as blatant violations of Pakistan's national sovereignty and territorial integrity. The protest reflected growing frustration within the Pakistani government over the continued use of drone strikes by the United States within its borders, even as both nations continued to grapple with the shared threat posed by militant groups operating in the region.

## Precedent-Setting Strike in Bannu

The wave of drone activity did not occur in isolation. An earlier strike on the preceding Wednesday had targeted the Bannu region, killing five people and wounding seven others. This attack was particularly notable because it reached farther into Pakistani territory than previous drone strikes had typically ventured, signaling a potential shift in the geographic scope of U.S. drone operations and raising fresh concerns in Islamabad about the expanding reach of these attacks beyond the traditionally targeted tribal areas.

Together, these incidents painted a picture of a nation under siege from multiple fronts—facing external pressure from U.S. drone operations while simultaneously contending with internal militant violence targeting civilian spaces such as mosques and public gatherings.

# U.S.-Pakistan Relations Strained Amid Continued Drone Strike Controversy

**ISLAMABAD** — Tensions between the United States and Pakistan have escalated further this week as officials from both countries traded pointed statements over the contentious issue of American drone strikes in Pakistan's tribal regions.

Prime Minister Yousuf Raza Gilani reiterated Pakistan's formal objection to the strikes, calling them a violation of national sovereignty and counterproductive to the broader fight against extremism. "These unilateral actions undermine the trust between our two nations and complicate our joint efforts against terrorism," Gilani said in a statement to parliament. "Pakistan's territorial integrity must be respected."

The Prime Minister's comments come amid mounting domestic political pressure, with opposition lawmakers and religious parties demanding a harder line against what they characterize as violations of Pakistani airspace. Public anger has also been fueled by reports of civilian casualties in recent strikes targeting militant strongholds in North Waziristan.

In response, the U.S. Ambassador defended the strikes as a necessary component of the broader counterterrorism strategy, emphasizing the shared threat posed by militant networks operating along the Afghanistan-Pakistan border. "We remain committed to working closely with our Pakistani partners," the ambassador stated, "but we cannot ignore the imperative to target those who pose a direct threat to both American and Pakistani security."

The ambassador further suggested that intelligence-sharing between the two nations had, in some instances, informed strike locations — a claim that has proven politically awkward for Islamabad, given the public's overwhelmingly negative view of the program.

Analysts note that the disagreement reflects a deeper structural tension in the bilateral relationship: while Pakistani officials publicly condemn the strikes, private cooperation between intelligence agencies has reportedly continued in some capacity. This dynamic has fueled accusations of hypocrisy from critics on both sides.

Regional experts warn that continued strikes without greater transparency or consultation risk further destabilizing an already fragile partnership. "Islamabad needs to show its public that sovereignty is being respected, while Washington needs Pakistani cooperation on the ground," said one South Asia policy analyst. "Finding that balance is proving increasingly difficult."

Neither government has indicated plans for a formal renegotiation of the terms governing the drone program, though both sides have signaled openness to further diplomatic talks in the coming weeks.

# CNN Report: U.S. Drone Strike Hits Militant Compound in North Waziristan

**ISLAMABAD, Pakistan** — A U.S. Predator drone strike targeted a suspected militant compound in Pakistan's North Waziristan tribal region early this morning, according to Pakistani intelligence officials who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the operation publicly.

## The Strike

Officials said the missile strike hit a compound near Miranshah, the main town in North Waziristan, an area long considered a stronghold for al Qaeda-linked militants and Taliban fighters operating on both sides of the Afghanistan-Pakistan border. Initial reports from local tribal sources suggested multiple casualties, though exact numbers remained unclear and could not be independently verified due to restricted media access in the region.

Pakistani security officials said they believed the target was a compound associated with foreign militants, though the identities of those killed had not been confirmed by mid-morning.

The Central Intelligence Agency, which operates the drone program in Pakistan's tribal areas, does not publicly comment on individual strikes, maintaining its longstanding policy of neither confirming nor denying specific operations.

## Pattern of Recent Strikes

This attack is the latest in a series of drone strikes that have intensified in the tribal regions bordering Afghanistan. U.S. officials have periodically described the campaign as targeting high-value al Qaeda and Taliban operatives, including bomb-makers and commanders believed responsible for attacks against U.S. and coalition forces in Afghanistan.

Previous strikes in the region have drawn both praise and condemnation. American officials have credited the program with killing several senior militant figures over the years, while critics — including human rights organizations — have raised persistent concerns about civilian casualties and the lack of transparency surrounding the strikes.

## Pakistani Government Response

The Pakistani Foreign Ministry issued a statement condemning the strike as a violation of the country's sovereignty, a response consistent with its public position on nearly all such attacks.

"We have repeatedly conveyed to the United States that these unilateral strikes are counterproductive, violate Pakistan's sovereignty, and undermine our joint efforts against terrorism," the ministry statement read.

This public condemnation, however, has long existed alongside what numerous former U.S. and Pakistani officials have described as tacit cooperation between the two governments — a dynamic that has fueled skepticism both domestically and internationally about the sincerity of Islamabad's objections.

Pakistani parliamentarians from opposition parties, as well as religious and nationalist political groups, renewed calls for the government to take a harder line against Washington, with some demanding Pakistan cut NATO supply lines running through its territory in protest.

## Regional and Political Fallout

Anti-American sentiment, already high in parts of Pakistan, is likely to be further inflamed by the strike. Local tribal leaders in North Waziristan have previously reported that such attacks stoke recruitment for militant groups and deepen resentment toward both Washington and Islamabad.

Analysts note that the drone program remains one of the most contentious issues in the U.S.-Pakistan relationship, complicating broader counterterrorism cooperation at a time when both governments have publicly emphasized the need for coordination against shared militant threats.

The Pakistani military has not commented on whether it received advance notice of the strike, a question that has surrounded past incidents and remains central to ongoing debate over the true extent of cooperation between the two nations.
